result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.latapy_clustering()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the bipartite clustering coefficient of each node (Latapy et al.). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L11836-L11929){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.latapy_clustering( nodes=None, mode="dot", ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Latapy bipartite clustering](/assets/graphs/latapy-clustering.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="People ann, bob and cy on top and the events party, talk and game below, all teal. Each person is shaded by the mean Jaccard overlap of their events with those of the people two steps away. ann and bob attended the same two events (overlap 1) and share one of cy's three (1/3), so both score 0.67; cy overlaps each of them by 1/3 and scores 0.33." width="100%"} A bipartite graph has no triangles, so the usual clustering coefficient is always zero. Latapy, Magnien and Del Vecchio (2008) measure clustering instead by how much a node's neighborhood overlaps with the neighborhoods of nodes two steps away (on its own side): two authors who share many papers, or two customers who bought the same products, have overlapping neighborhoods. The coefficient of a node is the average overlap with all nodes at distance two, which shows how cohesive its local bipartite neighborhood is. The overlap of two neighborhoods $N(u)$ and $N(v)$ is chosen by `mode=`: - `"dot"` (default): $|N(u) \cap N(v)| / |N(u) \cup N(v)|$ (Jaccard) - `"min"`: $|N(u) \cap N(v)| / \min(|N(u)|, |N(v)|)$ - `"max"`: $|N(u) \cap N(v)| / \max(|N(u)|, |N(v)|)$ Edge direction and parallel edges are ignored. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Union[int, str]] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional nodes (IDs or labels) to report. If `None` (default), all nodes. [mode]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["dot"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : `"dot"` (default), `"min"` or `"max"`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, float]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Node ID to its clustering coefficient, between 0 and 1. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is not bipartite, `mode` is unknown, or a node does not exist. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} For each node, the second neighborhood is collected and every pair is compared with set operations, $O(\sum_v \sum_{u \in N_2(v)} \deg)$ overall. Matches NetworkX's `bipartite.latapy_clustering` (also called `bipartite.clustering`). ## Examples {.doc-examples} Two people who attended the same two events have identical neighborhoods, while a third shares only one event with them: ::: {#7e5c0a33 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["ann", "bob", "cy", "party", "talk", "game"]) g.add_edges( [("ann", "party"), ("ann", "talk"), ("bob", "party"), ("bob", "talk"), ("cy", "talk"), ("cy", "game")] ) cc = g.latapy_clustering(nodes=["ann", "bob", "cy"]) {g.get_label_from_id(n): round(c, 3) for n, c in cc.items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'ann': 0.667, 'bob': 0.667, 'cy': 0.333} ``` ::: :::
